To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the natural invariant technique allows the integration of interactive theorem proving with automated theorem proving, and that it is possible to develop a methodology that allows the automatic discharge of most of the verification conditions, and to isolate the remaining difficult ones as lemmas that can be proved interactively.

(1) a natural invariant can be used to link the reference implementation level and the interactive verification process, (2) a natural invariant is a useful tool to guide the proof construction process, (3) the natural invariant is used as a specification of the program equivalence to be proved, and (4) a natural invariant allows the use of interactive proof techniques to prove program equivalences.

• A natural invariant-based methodology can be successfully used for proving program equivalences in an automatic/interactive setting, where the automatic part is based on the use of an automatic theorem prover.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the verification of the correctness of cryptographic software with respect to reference implementations.
the development of techniques for the verification of cryptographic software with respect to a specification.

the following questions: (1) how to specify cryptographic software, (2) how to check program equivalency, (3) how to integrate interactive proof techniques in a verification environment, and (4) how to check the correctness of cryptographic software implementations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have developed a practical and effective method to prove the equivalence of two programs in the presence of a large amount of unstructured code, and in the presence of non-determinism, concurrency and data races.

the techniques developed allow for the automatic verification of cryptographic programs with respect to reference implementations, and that this can be done in a manner that allows for the integration of the interactive proof techniques in the verification process.
this paper presents an integrated framework that combines the best of two worlds, namely, the best of interactive proof techniques and the best of automatic theorem provers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the techniques presented in this paper provide the means for verifying the equivalence between a cryptographic software and a reference implementation.
the techniques allow us to prove that a given program is equivalent to the reference implementation, and that this equivalence holds in all possible environments.
we have developed techniques for proving program equivalence in the context of software development for cryptographic systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, by isolating the difficult parts of a proof, the overall verification process becomes more manageable and more amenable to automation.
the verification process can be made more efficient by isolating the difficult parts of the verification problem and proving them interactively.
the use of interactive theorem provers can be greatly facilitated by the use of automatic theorem provers and the use of the natural invariant notion.
